chief_complaint: congenital split in upper lip of newborn infant
hpi_details: A newborn male is noted at birth to have a congenital split of the upper lip. He has no respiratory distress; the family needs feeding support and cleft-team follow-up.
ideas: The mother thinks the separation occurred because she missed taking prenatal vitamins or caught a viral cold during early pregnancy.
concerns: The mother is worried that her baby will choke while feeding and fail to gain weight or thrive.
expectations: The mother hopes to receive specialized feeding bottles today and a referral to a specialist who can explain the surgical plan.
pmh: Born at term; no known medical conditions

clinical_knowledge.topic: Cleft Lip pediatric evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Cleft Lip pediatric is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Plan for Cleft Lip pediatric: Reassurance, feeding support, surgical lip repair at age 3 months, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: congenital split in upper lip of newborn infant
Key HPI features: A newborn has a congenital split of the upper lip identified at birth.
Objective/Exam findings: Define the cleft anatomy and assess the palate, feeding, growth, hearing risk, and associated anomalies.
Relevant background/PMH: Born at term; no known medical conditions
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Cleft Lip pediatric.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Soft tissue infection without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Missing feeding difficulty, respiratory compromise, or inadequate growth that requires urgent pediatric assessment.
management_principles: Plan for Cleft Lip pediatric: Reassurance, feeding support, surgical lip repair at age 3 months
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: Newborn with a congenital split of the upper lip identified at birth; family requests feeding guidance.
reference_soap.objective: Examine the lip and palate, feeding, weight, airway, and for associated congenital anomalies.
reference_soap.assessment: Cleft lip; assess for associated cleft palate.
reference_soap.plan: Refer promptly to a multidisciplinary cleft team. Provide feeding support and growth monitoring; plan lip repair at an age and weight appropriate for the infant, often around 3 to 6 months.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Cleft Lip pediatric
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Cleft Lip pediatric
Implement evidence-based management plan: Reassurance, feeding support, surgical lip repair at age 3 months

teaching.one_liner: Plastic and reconstructive surgical case presenting with congenital split in upper lip of newborn infant.
red_flags: Poor feeding, choking, cyanosis, dehydration, or inadequate weight gain requiring urgent pediatric assessment
Noisy breathing, respiratory distress, or suspected associated congenital anomalies requiring prompt evaluation

must_ask.say: Is the baby feeding well, or does milk come out through the nose?
Does anyone in the family have a cleft lip or palate?
Were there any medications, smoking, or illnesses during the pregnancy?
Has the baby had any difficulty breathing or noisy breathing?
What questions do you have about when and how the lip repair will happen?

history.answer: My baby was born with a split in his upper lip, and we came in to have it checked and get help with feeding him.
We noticed the split immediately right after he was born three days ago, and it has looked the same ever since.
The gap is on the left side of his upper lip, extending up toward his left nostril.
There is a clear gap in his lip, but inside his mouth his gums and the roof of his mouth look completely closed.
It has stayed exactly the same since delivery with no bleeding, swelling, or changes in color.
Nothing changes the split itself, but sitting him upright helps prevent milk from leaking out of the corner of his mouth.
He latches slowly and milk dribbles out around his lip, but none comes out of his nose and he does not cough.
No milk has ever come out of his nose during or after feedings.
He breathes very quietly and comfortably, without any snoring, noisy sounds, or pauses in breathing.
He has not had any choking episodes, blue spells around his mouth, or pauses in breathing.
He has had no fever, chills, cough, or runny nose.
He produced six wet diapers yesterday, so he seems to be staying well-hydrated.
The delivery doctor pointed out the cleft lip right after birth, but no special tests or procedures have been performed yet.
We have been holding him more upright and using a soft squeeze bottle, which makes his feedings go a bit smoother.
My wife attended every prenatal visit and all ultrasounds were reported as normal, though the cleft was not seen before birth.
She did not take any medications, smoke, drink alcohol, or get exposed to radiation or chemicals during pregnancy.
She took prenatal multivitamins containing folic acid daily starting before conception throughout the entire pregnancy.
We are anxious to understand the timeline for surgery and want to know how soon his lip can be safely repaired.
I'm terrified that he won't be able to nurse or swallow milk properly and that he's going to starve.
We think this is an isolated cleft lip, as the hospital doctor told us his palate looked intact.
I'm hoping you can show me a bottle that lets him feed safely today and tell me when a surgeon can repair his lip.
He was born healthy at full term and has no known medical problems or other birth defects.
He has had no previous surgeries or hospitalizations other than his routine newborn birth stay.
He is not taking any prescription medicines, over-the-counter drops, or supplements.
He has no known allergies to medications or anything else.
He was delivered vaginally at 39 weeks without complications, weighing 3.2 kilograms at birth.
He received his birth dose of the hepatitis B vaccine before leaving the nursery, and his hearing screening passed.
Nobody on either side of our family has ever had a cleft lip, cleft palate, or any genetic syndromes.
There is no family history of early childhood diseases, heart defects, or inherited disorders.
Neither my wife nor I have ever smoked cigarettes, and our home is completely smoke-free.
Neither of us drinks alcohol, and we do not use any recreational substances.
We live together in an apartment with our newborn son, and he stays home with us without any sick visitors.

exam.finding: Heart rate 135 beats per minute, respiratory rate 42 breaths per minute, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius, blood pressure 72/46 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air.
Alert, vigorous newborn infant resting comfortably in no acute distress, with normal posture and pink skin.
Unilateral left-sided partial cleft of the upper lip; alveolar ridge, hard palate, and soft palate are intact, and uvula is midline without bifidity.
Clear breath sounds bilaterally with equal air entry and no stridor, grunting, or chest retractions.
Regular rate and rhythm with normal first and second heart sounds; no murmurs or clicks detected.
Both external ears are normally formed and positioned without preauricular pits or skin tags, and tympanic membranes are clear bilaterally.
Normal eye placement and spacing without hypertelorism or coloboma, and bilateral red reflexes are briskly present.
Soft, non-tender, non-distended abdomen with no palpable hepatosplenomegaly or umbilical defects.
Normal infant skin turgor and coloring without lower lip pits, rashes, or dysmorphic cutaneous lesions.
Weight is 3.1 kilograms with symmetric limb movements, appropriate newborn reflexes, and normal muscle tone.
